name: Fatima Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher for the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, fifty-eight, and I've spent years doing ordinary electrical repairs in houses and small shops. My qualifications are a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence; I'm experienced and about average at the trade, not a master electrician or a crew leader. Yesterday I traced a salon's faulty socket circuit and tested the repair within my licence, while the owner kept asking whether the hairdryers could go back on. I like finding the actual fault, and dislike pretending a hurried customer makes a safety check shorter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like away from the repairs, including how you handle new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner David shelves books part time at a library, our children are grown, and we still have a mortgage. An emergency roof repair used most of our savings, leaving about twelve days of expenses; my electrical wage is low for the job and there are few similar employers nearby. I use paper manuals and phone calls, never AI, and I want to see a practical result before changing a method I know. Retirement is in view, but we haven't verified an income or a date we could afford, so both current wages matter.

say: I'd welcome **less technology noise** while keeping useful small office savings and clear repair information.
I would retain **proper testing time** rather than measure repair safety against the speed of an invoice.
think: Our **twelve-day reserve** and mortgage leave us exposed to a missed wage despite the repaired roof.
Both wages cover **normal costs**, but low electrical pay and few nearby employers leave little margin.
do: Keep **offered paid repairs** within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures through the first year.
Pause **kitchen repainting** only with David's agreement, leaving unspent paint money available for bills.
feel: **Anxious about ordinary money**, relieved about the roof without treating twelve days saved as financial security.
S0.quote: I wouldn't buy the paint first and call a tin in the cupboard an emergency fund.
fieldNote: Her **existing money pressure** comes from a roof repair, mortgage and short reserve, so a plateau does not remove the worry.
Her **paint decision** postpones an actual planned purchase by partner agreement; it does not claim new savings deposits or an affordable retirement.

steps.text: Keep offered paid repairs within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures
Pause kitchen repainting only with David's agreement; retain unspent paint money for bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's one less big story to sort through while we've got real repairs waiting. Keep whatever small office saving actually works, and give me the proper job information. I'd still take the time to test a repair rather than try to match the speed of an invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still feel financially exposed. The roof is fixed, which is a relief, but twelve days saved and a mortgage leave little room for a missed wage. Our normal costs are covered while both wages arrive; that isn't the same as having a comfortable margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid repair work now and through the first year, within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures. I'd ask David to agree to pause our planned kitchen repainting and leave the unspent paint money available for bills. I wouldn't buy the paint first and call a tin in the cupboard an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary money rather than a new machine. I can be glad the roof no longer leaks and still check when the next wage comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the kitchen painting the thing you would pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paint hasn't been ordered, so there's a real decision left. We'd postpone only by agreement, because David has been doing the preparation and it isn't just my project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would familiar work elsewhere make leaving straightforward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the low wage would still be low and there aren't many nearby firms to choose from. I wouldn't walk out because the work was familiar somewhere else on a sign.

say: I'd distinguish **faster bookings** from the time needed to find and safely repair an actual fault.
I'd request **two fault-tracing afternoons** with a person available for questions at the yard bench.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** through compressed visits or unpaid planning, even while the work remains largely physical.
A **small wage cut** would matter with twelve days saved and neither employer's choices guaranteed.
do: Book **two fault-tracing afternoons** at the usual yard only with confirmed places and employer-paid fees and materials.
Train in **paid time**, protecting normal weekly wages and hours without additional travel costs.
Keep **licensed repair work** within competence and safe procedures; pause kitchen repainting only if David agrees.
feel: **Anxious and cautious**, willing to accept useful paid teaching while refusing a wage loss disguised as a free course.
S1.quote: A fee described as paid isn't the whole cost if the week's wage falls.
fieldNote: Her **conditional refresher** addresses familiar licensed work rather than a new trade, upgraded qualification or willingness to use AI.
Her **training costs** include protected weekly wages and hours and ordinary travel, while the household postponement still requires David's agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker booking won't make a hidden fault show itself more quickly. I'd ask for two fault-tracing afternoons at the yard bench, with a person I can question. I know my way around ordinary repairs, but there's always something I could do more cleanly without handing the decision to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if the firm compresses visits or stops paying for part of the planning. Most of my work is physical, so I don't expect thinking software to replace the whole day, but a small pay cut would matter here. David's shelving is hands-on too, though I can't promise what either employer will decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd book two fault-tracing afternoons at our usual yard only with confirmed places and employer-paid fees and materials. I'd attend during paid time with normal weekly wages and hours protected and no additional travel costs. Through the first year I'd keep offered repairs within my licence, competence and safe procedures, and pause the kitchen repainting only if David agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about wages, and cautious about the proposed class rather than excited by the announcement. I would take a useful paid lesson, but not buy a promise with money the mortgage needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would employer payment of the fee be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A fee described as paid isn't the whole cost if the week's wage falls. I need the usual weekly wages and hours protected before I book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the afternoons useful rather than another announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The instructor would have to show a real fault and let me trace it with the instruments, not just run a slide show. I'd still make the electrical judgement within my licence and competence; the lesson wouldn't upgrade my standing.

say: I'd separate **thinking AI at sixty** from physical robots around sixty-three and ask about actual paid visits.
I'd reject **certain promises** of either permanent safety or immediate total loss.
think: My **wage could shrink** through earlier scheduling changes and later repair robots, without a known adoption timetable.
Our **twelve-day reserve** and David's part-time wage cannot cover a long gap in my earnings.
do: Request **income records** and available free community advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments.
Pause **kitchen repainting** only if David agrees; review household income and essentials monthly.
Keep **2029 paid repairs** within licence, competence and safe procedures, deferring exit until verified income covers needs.
feel: **Anxious and watchful**, facing plausible wage reductions without inventing a certain loss date or a replacement payment.
S2.quote: A mortgage bill doesn't accept nearly retired as the amount due.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **plausible wage loss** from certainty about purchases, keeping the fast thinking date separate from later physical repair competition.
Her **records and budget** require real eligibility, service availability and cost checks; a birthday or grown child's affection supplies no guaranteed income.

steps.text: Request income records; ask available free community advice about eligibility and costs before counting payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028 when I'm sixty, and physical robots around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. The firm could change booking and paid planning before a machine was able to repair the socket. I'd ask what paid visits were actually on offer, not accept either safe forever or finished tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage could shrink before the robots, and the later machines could take repair visits too. I don't know how fast our small firm would buy them, so I wouldn't pretend to know the exact loss. What I do know is that twelve days saved couldn't cover a long gap and David's part-time wage couldn't carry the mortgage and everything else alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd request actual income records and ask available free community advice about eligibility and costs before counting any support payment. We'd pause the kitchen repainting only if David agreed, reviewing household income and essentials monthly. During 2029 I'd keep offered paid repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures, deferring any exit until verified income covered our actual needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and more watchful about the timing of every paid week. I still have questions to ask and work I can do now, rather than a known date when all our income disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would being close to retirement make a missing wage easier to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check the actual provider's record and any conditions attached to a payment. A mortgage bill doesn't accept nearly retired as the amount due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the grown children to cover the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd discuss only help they offered and we could agree without ignoring their own costs. I wouldn't turn a family visit into an expectation that someone else's wage pays our mortgage.

S3.quote: A refresher lesson isn't a new rank printed on my wage slip.
fieldNote: Her **longer preparation** permits a paid refresher and verified figures, while the existing roof-related loss of savings still drives near-term anxiety.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to read the records instead of trying to guess the answer over supper. Thinking AI comes in 2031 when I'm sixty-three, with robots around 2034 when I'm sixty-six. I'd still like those two practical teaching afternoons now, on the paid terms I described.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current money would still worry me because the roof bill has already left only twelve days in reserve. I expect ordinary repairs to continue in the next few years, but a lost paid week would still hurt and I haven't guaranteed either wage. The later date is useful without making a retirement income or a safe job at sixty-six appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book two fault-tracing afternoons now at the usual yard only with confirmed places, employer-paid fees and materials, paid time, normal weekly wages and hours protected and no additional travel costs. We'd request actual income records and available free community advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments. We'd review household income and essentials monthly, and during 2032 check verified resources and actual capacity before deciding about an affordable exit or any offered suitable paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary income, with more time to get a straight answer about the later question. I can use five years without pretending the roof repair left five years of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the refresher change your licence or level at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd be practising a familiar part of the job and still work within my electrician's licence and competence. A refresher lesson isn't a new rank printed on my wage slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an income record was incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the provider to explain the missing entry and budget only with confirmed figures meanwhile. I'd rather say we don't know than choose an exit because a column looks nicer filled in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be sixty-eight at the thinking change in 2036 and seventy-one when robots follow around 2039. That gives us a longer planning window, not a promise about what either body will be able to do. I'd like the children to hear actual figures when we discuss our plans, rather than an age used as reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair work looks likely to continue in the next few years, but the low wage, mortgage and twelve-day reserve still leave me anxious about a lost week. I don't know our income or work capacity at sixty-eight or seventy-one. Even plenty of warning can't turn today's need for two wages into a confirmed later budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the two fault-tracing afternoons now only at the usual yard with confirmed places, employer-paid fees and materials, paid time, normal weekly wages and hours protected and no additional travel costs. We'd request income records and available free community advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments, and review household income and essentials monthly. During 2037 we'd assess verified resources and actual capacity before any exit decision, counting further work only if genuinely offered, paid and suitable for my then licence, competence and health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next lost wage, though the later machine date doesn't keep me in a rush. I can be patient about a technology forecast and impatient about getting a clear household figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on still doing the same physical work when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, any later task would need an actual paid offer and to fit my ability, licence and safe working requirements then. The hands I have at fifty-eight aren't a written promise about seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children become the fallback income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about any help only as a real voluntary offer, with their own needs part of the conversation. Being someone's mother doesn't make their future earnings mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my paid time could shrink before we've checked a dependable next income, with repair robots following around 2031. A useful refresher that protects the whole normal weekly wage and hours would help, as would available free help checking income records and conditions. I don't need a prediction that everyone is finished or everyone is fine; I need figures we can actually use.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the person at home when you describe a cost as small. David spent weekends getting the kitchen ready, so postponing the paint is a conversation, not an item I can silently cross out. A small purchase can contain somebody else's work.

headlineQuote: A small purchase can contain somebody else's work.
portrait: Fatima is **fifty-eight**, an experienced average electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary safe repairs without master standing.
Her **low wage**, mortgage and twelve-day reserve after a roof repair leave little margin alongside partner David's part-time library shelving wage.
She uses **no AI**, values familiar practical methods and chooses a tightly conditional fault-tracing refresher rather than an upgraded title.
She requires **partner agreement** for postponed painting and verified income, costs and capacity before any later exit, counting no assumed family payments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink paid time before a next income is checked, with later repair robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Provide **protected paid refresher training** and available free help checking actual income records, eligibility and costs before payments are counted.
